## Objectives {.unnumbered}

This lab accompanies the Week 8 notes, [*Introduction to Shiny*](https://soton-fds.github.io/week08.html).

- Build and run a Shiny app from an `R` script.
- Add input widgets (`textInput`, `numericInput`, `selectInput`) to an app, and display their values with output widgets and render functions.
- Use a reactive expression to compute a value that outputs depend on.
- Build an interactive data visualiser with `ggplot2`.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions in `lab_08_practice.qmd`, including why reactive expressions matter, observers and buttons, exploring the penguins data with your visualiser, and deploying an app to `shinyapps.io` so that other people can use it.

## About the Lab

In this lab you will write most of your code in `R` scripts, not in this Quarto document.
As in the Week 8 notes, we always write Shiny apps in `R` scripts: a rendered Quarto document is a static web page, with no `R` process behind it to run an app.
Write all your Shiny apps in the `src/` subdirectory.
Write your answers to the written questions in the solution boxes in this document.

To run an app, open its script in RStudio and click the **Run App** button above the editor (see [Running Shiny Apps](https://soton-fds.github.io/week08.html#running-shiny-apps) in the Week 8 notes).
While the app is running, your `R` console is busy serving it: stop the app with the stop icon in the console (or `Esc`) to get your prompt back.
A running app does not pick up changes to its script, so after editing an app, save it and click **Run App** again.

### Task 1: A First App

- [ ] Open the file `src/app1.R`
- [ ] Run the shiny app.
- [ ] Add a `textOutput` to the `ui` which the `server` fills with a greeting using the name that has been entered: for example, "Hello Ada" if the name is Ada.
- [ ] Add a `numericInput` to the `ui` for the user to input their age. Make the UI print the age somewhere.
- [ ] Look up the [`selectInput` control](https://shiny.posit.co/r/reference/shiny/latest/selectinput.html). Add a `selectInput` control that lets you choose a favourite colour from a list. Make the UI print the selected colour somewhere.
- [ ] **Extension:** Look up the `renderUI` function and use it to change the colour of the greeting to the chosen colour.

#### Hint: Using renderUI to change greeting colour

To dynamically change the colour of the greeting based on the selected colour, use `renderUI` in the server and `uiOutput` in the UI.
`renderUI` can return HTML tags such as `span`, whose `style` argument sets the CSS used to display it.
For example, this displays some text in blue:

```r
# In the ui:
uiOutput("coloured_text")

# In the server:
output$coloured_text <- renderUI({
  span(style = "color: blue;", "Some blue text")
})
```

#### Before a Name Is Entered

- [ ] Restart your app, and look at the heading and the greeting before you type a name. What do they show?
- [ ] Use `req()` (see the Week 8 notes) so that the heading is just "Shiny App", and no greeting is displayed, until a name has been entered. Where is the best place to put the `req()` for the greeting?

::: {.solution}

:::

#### The Reactive Graph

Now look at how the parts of your finished app depend on each other.

- [ ] Using the Reactive Programming section of the [Week 8 notes](https://soton-fds.github.io/week08.html), list the sources, conductors and endpoints in your app, and sketch its reactive graph.
- [ ] Which endpoints re-run when the user changes only the colour? Which re-run when they change only the name?

::: {.solution}

:::

### Task 2: A Data Visualiser

The file `src/data/penguins.csv` contains the penguins data from the Week 8 notes: body measurements of 344 penguins of three species, recorded on three islands in Antarctica between 2007 and 2009.
Write a new app in `src/` that is a flexible visualiser for this data.

As in the data explorer in the Week 8 notes, read the data once, before the `ui`, rather than inside the server.
When Shiny runs an app, it uses the app's own folder (here `src/`) as the working directory, so the app should read `"data/penguins.csv"`, not `"src/data/penguins.csv"`.
(If you run the script line by line in the console instead, the working directory is the project folder, so the same path will not be found.)

The visualiser should allow the user to:

- Select numerical variables for the $x$ and $y$ axes of a plot (using `selectInput`) and render the plot. *Hint: a `selectInput` gives you a string, such as `"bill_length_mm"`, rather than a column. Inside `aes()`, `.data[[input$x_var]]` refers to the column whose name is stored in `input$x_var`.*
- Select a categorical variable to use to colour the points on the plot.
- Enter friendly $x$- and $y$-axis labels, and a title.
- Create a `reactive` expression that filters the dataset based on another categorical variable.

Once your app can filter the data:

- [ ] Plot body mass against flipper length for Adelie penguins only, then for Gentoo penguins only. Compare the two plots: how could they mislead someone comparing the two species?
- [ ] Change your app so that the axes stay the same whatever is filtered. (Hint: see how the data explorer in the Week 8 notes fixes its axes. Here, the limits need to depend on the variables chosen.)

::: {.solution}

:::
